result: Yeast mother cells form a single, stable age-associated protein deposit early in replicative aging (after 3-4 divisions) that is asymmetrically inherited by the mother cell with high fidelity (98% of divisions). The deposit forms rapidly, becomes stable within hours, persists until late life, and displays limited exchange with the cytoplasm (59% immobile Hsp104). This phenomenon is general across strain backgrounds, ploidy levels, and independent of experimental procedures.
evaluation: Claims C1, C19, C26-C37 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (MEP, microfluidics, FRAP, time-lapse imaging) showing consistent deposit formation kinetics, stability, inheritance patterns, and generalizability across conditions. The quantitative data on timing, inheritance fidelity, and protein dynamics are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and controls.

result: The age-associated protein deposit has a specific chaperone composition: Hsp70 proteins (Ssa1, Ssa2), Hsp42, and Hsp40 protein Ydj1 readily localize to deposits, while Hsp26 is enriched in only 15% of deposits, and Sis1 and Hsp82 are excluded.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by systematic co-localization analysis with quantitative data (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C). The differential localization patterns are clearly documented with appropriate sample sizes and provide important characterization of deposit composition.

result: The prion protein Sup35 accumulates in age-associated deposits in a prion-state dependent manner: 33% of [PSI+] cells with deposits show Sup35 accumulation, while [psi−] cells show none. Sup35 accumulation is age-dependent and the Sup35-enriched deposits segregate asymmetrically to mother cells (98% of mitoses). The [PSI+] state does not affect overall deposit formation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by quantitative co-localization data, time-lapse imaging, and segregation analysis (Figure 2A-G). The prion-state specificity is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls ([psi−] cells), and the asymmetric inheritance is well-documented.

result: The P-body component Dcp2 does not accumulate in age-associated deposits and P-bodies never fuse with age-associated deposits, even under conditions that induce P-body formation.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by co-localization data under multiple conditions including P-body induction (Figure 2H-J). The complete absence of co-localization (0/57 foci) and lack of fusion events provide strong evidence for distinct compartments.

result: Age-associated protein deposits are distinct from previously characterized protein quality control compartments (Q-bodies, JUNQ/INQ, IPOD). Q-bodies are transient and reversible, while age-associated deposits are stable. Chaperone composition differs: Hsp82 and Btn2 localize to Q-bodies but not age-associated deposits. VHL (JUNQ/INQ marker) and Rnq1 (IPOD marker) form separate structures that do not co-localize with age-associated deposits in >87-98% of cases.
evaluation: Claims C46-C54 provide systematic comparative analysis with quantitative data distinguishing age-associated deposits from other compartments based on dynamics, chaperone composition, and marker localization (Figure 3). The high percentages of non-co-localization (87-98.6%) with appropriate sample sizes support the conclusion of distinct structures.

result: Deposit formation is not associated with general proteostasis decline or stress. Aged cells with deposits clear heat-induced protein aggregates (Q-bodies) as efficiently as young cells (71±5 min vs 72±4 min, n.s.). Cells with and without pre-existing deposits show comparable Q-body responses to heat stress. Mild proteotoxic stress counteracts deposit formation.
evaluation: Claims C2, C4, C55, C56, C58 are supported by quantitative time-lapse analysis of Q-body clearance and formation under controlled conditions (Figure 4). The lack of significant difference in clearance times and the unexpected protective effect of mild stress are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and controls.

result: Cells with age-associated deposits display enhanced degradation of cytosolic UPS substrates (rate constant K: 0.155±0.007 vs 0.129±0.006, p<0.01) but show no difference in nuclear UPS substrate degradation (K: 0.075±0.004 vs 0.079±0.005, n.s.), indicating compartment-specific enhancement of proteostasis.
evaluation: Claims C3, C59-C61 are supported by quantitative auxin-inducible degron assays with appropriate statistical analysis and sample sizes (N=91 cells per category for cytosolic, N=65-66 for nuclear) (Figure 5). The compartment-specific effect is demonstrated by differential results between cytosolic and nuclear substrates.

result: Age-associated deposit formation is dependent on Hsp42, which is the first protein to mark the structure (24/25 cells), appearing before Hsp104 and Ssa1 (up to 120 min earlier). Deletion of HSP42 abolishes deposit formation, while overexpression causes precocious nucleation and growth. Hsp104 and Hsp70 (Ssa1/Ssa2) oppose deposit formation: their deletion accelerates deposit formation, while Hsp104 overexpression reduces deposits and destabilizes them.
evaluation: Claims C5, C62-C71 are supported by time-lapse imaging, genetic deletion/overexpression studies with quantitative analysis (Figure 6). The temporal ordering (24/25 cells), complete abolishment by HSP42 deletion, and opposing effects of Hsp104/Hsp70 provide strong mechanistic evidence.

result: The hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double mutant shows severely impaired deposit formation with cells crowded with punctate Ssa1-GFP speckles that fail to coalesce. An in vivo reconstitution assay demonstrates that simultaneous reintroduction of Hsp104 and Hsp42 clears speckles within 5 min, Hsp42 alone forms a single focus, while Hsp104 alone shows slow incomplete clearance.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by microscopy of double mutants and a clever reconstitution assay using mating to rapidly reintroduce chaperones (Figure 7). The differential effects of reintroducing individual vs. both chaperones provide strong mechanistic insight into their opposing roles.

result: Loss of Hsp42 results in symmetric inheritance of protein aggregates. While wild-type and hsp104Δ cells retain deposits in mothers with 98% fidelity, hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double mutants show frequent inheritance by daughters (>65% of buds contain aggregates vs <4% in other genotypes).
evaluation: Claims C7, C79-C82 are supported by quantitative analysis of aggregate inheritance in buds across genotypes with large sample sizes (96-186 divisions for wild-type/hsp104Δ, appropriate samples for double mutants) (Figure 8A-B). The dramatic difference in bud inheritance (>65% vs <4%) is statistically robust.

result: Loss of Hsp42 extends replicative lifespan by >40% (39 vs 27 generations for wild-type, p<0.001), while hsp104Δ mutants are short-lived (21.5 generations, p<0.001). The hsp104Δ hsp42Δ double mutant lifespan (23 generations) is similar to hsp104Δ alone and significantly shorter than wild-type or hsp42Δ.
evaluation: Claims C8, C83-C85 are supported by replicative lifespan analysis with appropriate sample sizes (N=101-140 cells per genotype) and statistical significance testing (Figure 8C). The epistatic relationship between hsp104Δ and hsp42Δ is clearly demonstrated.

result: Protein aggregation is an early aging-associated differentiation event with a two-faceted role in organismal fitness: it can promote spatial protein quality control and may harbor epigenetic information (like Sup35 prion), but has negative long-term consequences for the aging lineage.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C89-C91 represent interpretive conclusions supported by the collective experimental evidence: early deposit formation (C30), enhanced UPS function (C59), Sup35 storage (C38-C43), and shortened lifespan in wild-type vs hsp42Δ (C84). The two-faceted interpretation is reasonable given the data, though the beneficial aspects are observed in young cells and may not persist.

result: Overexpression of HSP42 has no effect on lifespan, suggesting wild-type Hsp42 levels are sufficient for maximal effects on lifespan, consistent with early deposit appearance in wild-type cells.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are based on unpublished data ("data not shown") and inference. While the interpretation is reasonable given early deposit formation in wild-type, the lack of presented data prevents full evaluation of experimental rigor, sample sizes, and statistical analysis.

result: The authors speculate that UPS function may decline later in aging, that increased available Sis1 might explain enhanced UPS function, and that there is a need to differentiate between pathophysiological and homeostatic protein aggregation.
evaluation: Claims C92, C95-C97 are explicitly speculative ("it is possible," "plausible," "might") and represent discussion points rather than experimental findings. While reasonable hypotheses, they lack direct experimental support and are appropriately presented as speculation requiring future work.

result: The age-associated protein deposit does not clearly match criteria for previously characterized deposits (Q-bodies, JUNQ/INQ, IPOD) but exists in parallel with JUNQ and IPOD. Pathological aggregation processes may hijack endogenous proteostasis mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by the comparative analysis in Figures 1 and 3 showing distinct properties from other compartments. The interpretation that pathological processes hijack endogenous mechanisms is reasonable inference from the data on VHL and Rnq1 overexpression.

result: Long-lived asymmetrically retained proteins (Hsp104, Ssa1, Ssa2, Hsp26) localize to age-associated deposits. Sup35 storage in deposits renders it inherited by mothers, consistent with size-dependent transmission. Aging does not enhance [PSI+] generation, suggesting Sup35 cannot escape deposits under normal conditions, though heat shock can temporarily disassemble deposits, potentially allowing prion spread.
evaluation: Claims C101-C106 integrate current findings with prior literature. The overlap with long-lived proteins is supported by comparison with Thayer et al. 2014 (C101). Sup35 inheritance (C102) is demonstrated in Figure 2. The inability to escape (C104) is inference supported by FRAP data (C36) and citations. Heat-induced disassembly (C105) is shown in Figure 4. The speculation about environmental triggering (C106) is appropriately tentative.

result: Background claims about aging, asymmetric inheritance, and protein aggregation in yeast and other organisms, establishing the context for the study.
evaluation: Claims C11-C18 are background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Supporting claims from prior literature: Hsp42 overexpression promotes [PSI+] curing while deletion enhances induction; fission yeast use similar Hsp16-dependent mechanisms; polyQ disease models show Sis1 sequestration; asymmetric inheritance appears conserved in metazoan stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C77-C78, C88, C93-C94, C103, C107-C108 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Duennwald et al. 2012, Coelho et al. 2014, Park et al. 2013, Shewmaker and Wickner 2006, Rujano et al. 2006, Bufalino et al. 2013). These contextualize the current findings within existing literature.
